Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let  
\[
k=\lfloor \sqrt n\rfloor,
\]
so
\[
k^2\le n<(k+1)^2.
\]

We will show that any solution \(n\ge 6\) is at most \(1230\), and then verify that \(1230\) actually works.

---

### 1. Prime factors \(\le k\)

Suppose \(p^a\| n\) and \(p\le k\). Then \(p\mid k!\), so
\[
(k!)^{n!}
\]
is divisible by \(p^{n!}\). Since \(a\le \log_2 n<n!\) for \(n\ge 6\), we have \(p^a\mid (k!)^{n!}\). Therefore
\[
(k!)^{n!}+450\equiv 450 \pmod{p^a}.
\]
If \(n\) divides the given expression, then \(p^a\mid 450\). Thus every prime-power part of \(n\) whose prime is \(\le k\) must divide
\[
450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2.
\]

So the part of \(n\) composed of primes \(\le k\) divides \(450\).

---

### 2. Prime factors \(>k\)

First, \(n\) cannot contain two distinct prime factors both greater than \(k\), because then
\[
n\ge (k+1)(k+2)>(k+1)^2,
\]
contradicting \(n<(k+1)^2\). Also, no such prime can appear to a power at least \(2\), since if \(p>k\), then
\[
p^2\ge (k+1)^2>n.
\]

Hence there is at most one prime \(r>k\), and it appears to the first power.

Now suppose such a prime \(r\mid n\). Since \(r\le n\), the integer \(r-1\) divides \(n!\). Also \(r>k\), so \(\gcd(k!,r)=1\). By Fermat’s theorem,
\[
(k!)^{r-1}\equiv 1\pmod r.
\]
Because \(r-1\mid n!\),
\[
(k!)^{n!}\equiv 1\pmod r.
\]
Thus
\[
(k!)^{n!}+450\equiv 451\pmod r.
\]
So \(r\mid 451=11\cdot 41\). Therefore the only possible prime factor \(>k\) is \(11\) or \(41\).

---

### 3. Bounding \(n\)

Let \(m\) be the part of \(n\) made from primes \(\le k\). From step 1, \(m\mid 450\).

There are three cases:

- If \(n\) has no prime factor \(>k\), then \(n=m\le 450\).
- If the large prime is \(11\), then \(11>k\), so
  \[
  n=11m<11^2=121.
  \]
  Hence \(m<11\). The largest divisor of \(450\) less than \(11\) is \(10\), so
  \[
  n\le 11\cdot 10=110.
  \]
- If the large prime is \(41\), then \(41>k\), so
  \[
  n=41m<41^2=1681.
  \]
  Hence \(m<41\). The largest divisor of \(450\) less than \(41\) is \(30\), so
  \[
  n\le 41\cdot 30=1230.
  \]

Thus every solution \(n\ge 6\) satisfies
\[
n\le 1230.
\]

---

### 4. Verification that \(n=1230\) works

For \(n=1230\),
\[
k=\lfloor \sqrt{1230}\rfloor=35,
\]
and
\[
1230=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 41.
\]

Since \(35!\) is divisible by \(2,3,5\), the number
\[
(35!)^{1230!}
\]
is divisible by \(30=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\). Also \(450\) is divisible by \(30\), so their sum is divisible by \(30\).

For the factor \(41\), note that \(\gcd(35!,41)=1\) and \(40\mid 1230!\). By Fermat’s theorem,
\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 1\pmod{41}.
\]
Therefore
\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 1+450=451\equiv 0\pmod{41}.
\]

Thus \(30\mid (35!)^{1230!}+450\) and \(41\mid (35!)^{1230!}+450\). Since \(\gcd(30,41)=1\),
\[
30\cdot 41=1230
\]
divides the expression.

Hence the largest possible positive integer is

\[
\boxed{1230}
\]
